required_facts_checked: The study analyzed more than 1,000 job descriptions and classified 889 into three categories.
AI-first roles were about 70 percent and worked on LLM/GenAI systems, RAG, agents, evaluation and production deployment.
AI-support roles were about 28.5 percent and focused on infrastructure and platforms around AI.
Traditional ML/DL roles were under 2 percent and used standard ML or deep-learning tools under the AI Engineer title.
The practical definition centered on owning foundation-model system design, evaluation and production operation.
Roles were 95.6 percent production-focused, nearly 50 percent backend-heavy and 20 percent often full-stack.
RAG appeared in 35.9 percent, prompt engineering in 29.1 percent, LLM integration in 25.4 percent, agents in 14.4 percent and fine-tuning in 8.5 percent.
Python appeared in 82.5 percent, with TypeScript at 23.4 percent, React at 14.8 percent and FastAPI at 10.7 percent.
Operations and cloud appeared in 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent; AWS, Docker, CI/CD and Kubernetes formed a common infrastructure baseline.
Classical ML accounted for 9.5 percent overall, with PyTorch at 22.0 percent and TensorFlow at 12.9 percent within that group.
The study's day-to-day layers include core end-to-end RAG and agent work, common retrieval/platform work and secondary frontend, performance, fine-tuning or security work.
Framework mentions were spread across LangChain, LangGraph and LlamaIndex, with no single framework dominating.
unsupported_claims_removed: Removed any implication that the dataset's percentages define every AI Engineer role or guarantee a hiring outcome.
Removed prescriptions for a specific framework and unsupported claims about framework longevity.
substantive_edits: Rewrote the article as a reader-facing explanation of the study's categories, skill frequencies and responsibility layers.
Preserved exact percentages while separating observed market signals from the practical definition drawn from them.
Explained why architecture and production fundamentals matter more than loyalty to one application framework.
